chunks: From him, from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Hammad, from Sa'id ibn Yasar, who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about a man who had intercourse with his slave-girl, who goes and comes (i.e., is not confined), and he had withdrawn (from her), and there had been no other act of his towards her. What do you say about the child? He said: I see that this should not be sold, O Sa'id. And I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), and he said: Do you accuse her? I said: As for an apparent accusation, no. He said: Do your people accuse her? I said: As for something apparent, no. He said: Then how can you manage for the child not to be attached to you? Because the reasoning in these two reports is that if the slave-girl is trodden upon (i.e., has intercourse) by him at every time, it is not fitting that he should disown her child due to the suspicion which is not conclusive. And what we said in the first two reports was permissible if his treading upon her was not except at times, and at times when it predominates in his opinion that the child is not from him, so the ruling regarding it is what we said.

key_terms.يَطَؤُهَا: he trod upon her (idiom for intercourse)
key_terms.يَلۡزَمَكَ ٱلۡوَلَدُ: the child is attached to you (paternity is established)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a child born to a slave-girl when the master has occasional intercourse with her?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani’s *al-Istibsar* elucidates the Shia legal principle of *al-waladu lil-firash* (the child follows the bed) by distinguishing between frequent and occasional intercourse to determine the strength of paternity suspicion (*zann*). The Imam clarifies that while frequent access creates an inseparable link to the father, occasional intercourse allows for disowning unless there is a clear, dominant suspicion of paternity, reflecting the juristic balance between certainty and probability in lineage attribution.
